label: Elam
pitch:
In the highlands and lowlands of southwestern Iran, the Elamites built one of the ancient world's most enduring civilizations — a perennial rival of Mesopotamia that outlasted Sumer, challenged Babylon, and fought Assyria for over two thousand years. From the Proto-Elamite Period around 2700 BCE to the final destruction by the Achaemenid Persians in 539 BCE, Elam carved its own path in the shadow of its better-known neighbors.

🔑 Key Facts:
• The Ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil, built by Untash-Napirisha around 1250 BCE, is the best-preserved ziggurat outside Mesopotamia and a UNESCO World Heritage Site
• The Proto-Elamite Script is one of the world's oldest undeciphered writing systems, predating even the earliest Sumerian tablets at some sites
• Shutruk-Nahhunte sacked Babylon in 1158 BCE and carried off the Code of Hammurabi and the Stele of Naram-Sin to Susa — where archaeologists found them 3,000 years later
• Susa, the Elamite capital, was continuously inhabited for over 6,000 years, making it one of the longest-lived cities in human history

🤔 Why It Matters: Elam demonstrates that Mesopotamia did not develop in isolation. The Elamites created their own writing, religion, and political systems, and their interactions — from trade to warfare — shaped the development of Babylonian and Assyrian civilization. The Elamite heartland later became the core of the Persian Empire.

🎲 Wild Card: When the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal finally destroyed Elam in 646 BCE during the Sack of Susa, he boasted of salting the fields and carrying off the bones of Elamite kings so their ghosts could find no rest. Yet within a century, the Persians rose from the same Iranian highlands to build the largest empire the world had ever seen.

spans.label: Proto-Elamite Period
spans.description: The earliest phase of Elamite statehood centered on Susa and Anshan, with the Dynasty of Awan maintaining independence from Akkadian and Sumerian empires. The undeciphered Proto-Elamite script was in use during this era.

spans.label: Old Elamite Period
spans.description: Elam sacked Ur in 2004 BCE and the Sukkalmah dynasty governed through a unique shared-power system. Elamite cuneiform adoption and expanding trade networks connected the Iranian highlands to Mesopotamia.

spans.label: Middle Elamite Period
spans.description: Elam's golden age under kings like Untash-Napirisha and Shutruk-Nahhunte, who built the ziggurat at Chogha Zanbil and sacked Babylon. The empire reached its greatest territorial extent under Shilhak-Inshushinak.

spans.label: Neo-Elamite Period
spans.description: A long decline punctuated by brief revivals, ending when Ashurbanipal sacked Susa in 646 BCE. Elamite culture survived through the Achaemenid Persians, who made Susa their capital and adopted Elamite administrative traditions.

events.label: Proto-Elamite Script
events.description: The Proto-Elamite script — one of the world's oldest writing systems, scratched onto clay tablets around 3100 BCE for bookkeeping, that spread across the Iranian plateau and, frustratingly, has never been cracked.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It appeared at almost the same moment as the first Sumerian writing next door, suggesting the two cultures lit the spark of literacy in dialogue rather than in isolation. The tablets are overwhelmingly accountants' records — tallies of grain, livestock, and workers — not poetry or prayer, a reminder that writing was invented to count things before it was ever used to tell stories. The reason it stays mute is brutal for scholars: there's no bilingual key like the Rosetta Stone, and the language behind the signs may be one we simply have no other trace of.

events.commonsFile: P1180316 Louvre Suse III tablette économique Sb15200 rwk.jpg

events.label: City of Anshan
events.description: Anshan (modern Tal-e Malyan) was Elam's highland capital, a huge walled city up in the cold mountain basins of Fars, about 160 miles (260 km) east of Susa. For centuries Elamite kings styled themselves rulers "of Anshan and Susa."

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Anshan was enormous — its walled area swelled to roughly 500 acres by 2700 BCE, putting it in the same size class as the biggest Sumerian cities while sitting a world away behind the Zagros ridges. Its location was actually lost to modern scholars: they knew the name "Anshan" from Mesopotamian and later Persian inscriptions but had no idea where it was until 1971, when archaeologists digging the mound of Tal-e Malyan found tablets that named the city. The highland world it ruled produced masterworks of early metal craft, like the famous Proto-Elamite silver bull statuettes that survive from this era.

events.commonsFile: Proto-Elamite kneeling bull holding a spouted vessel.jpg

events.label: Elamite Trade Networks
events.description: Elamite merchants were the middlemen of the Bronze Age, moving tin, copper, lapis, and carnelian between the Iranian highlands and the cities of southern Iraq. By 2500 BCE they show up in Mesopotamian records as the suppliers temples couldn't do without.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: This trade is why Elam and Mesopotamia could never truly cut each other off, even when at war: Mesopotamia needed the metals and stones only Elamite traders could deliver, and Elam needed Mesopotamian grain and finished goods in return. The same network stocked the dazzling treasures of the Royal Tombs of Ur, whose Afghan lapis and Indus carnelian were routed through the trade web Elam sat on top of. Burials at Susa contain necklaces assembling stones from the Indus, Central Asia, and northeastern Iran on a single string — a whole trade map worn around one neck.

events.commonsFile: Jewelry with components from the Indus, Central Asia and Northern-eastern Iran found in Susa dated to 2600-1700 BCE, SB 13099.jpg

events.label: Dynasty of Awan
events.description: The Dynasty of Awan was the first Elamite royal house we can name — twelve kings, ending with Puzur-Inshushinak — who held their highland kingdom together through a mix of treaty-making and mountain warfare while Sumer and Akkad rose and fell on the plain below.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: We know the line mostly from a single tablet: a king-list copied out at Susa centuries later that names twelve rulers of Awan (and twelve of the following Shimashki dynasty) in order. The names are mangled and several are barely legible, so much of the early dynasty is little more than a row of half-readable syllables — historians treat most of them as uncertain. "Awan" itself was a place whose exact location is still debated, which neatly captures how thin the ground is: Elam's first dynasty is real, but it reaches us through the winners' paperwork and one battered list.

events.commonsFile: Dynastic list Awan Siwashi Louvre Sb17729.jpg

events.label: City of Susa
events.description: Susa was the great lowland city of Elam, sitting on the hot Khuzestan plain where three rivers and the Zagros foothills meet. Settled around 4200 BCE, it is one of the oldest cities humans have never stopped living in.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Susa's first claim to fame is its pottery: thin, elegant beakers and dishes painted with bold geometric birds, ibexes, and hatched diamonds around 4000 BCE, now a signature of the Near Eastern Copper Age and a star of the Louvre. The city sat on so good a spot that it kept being rebuilt for over four thousand years, surviving repeated sackings by Mesopotamian and Assyrian armies who would declare it destroyed and then leave. Its acropolis mound is so deep with layered ruins that a 19th-century French archaeological mission built an actual castle on top of it to dig in safely.

events.commonsFile: Iran époque d'Obeid Sèvres.jpg

events.label: Cult of Inshushinak
events.description: Inshushinak — the name means "Lord of Susa" — was the patron god of the city and one of the chief gods of all Elam. He was a judge and an underworld figure who, Elamite texts suggest, received the soul of a king at his death.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His cult is one of the longest-running religious traditions in the entire region: documented from around 2500 BCE, still going at the Assyrian sack of Susa in 646 BCE, and traceable into the Persian period around 500 BCE — well over two thousand years of worship of a single city god. Kings swore their oaths in his name and built and rebuilt his temple at the heart of Susa. Elamite worshippers left striking votive offerings to him, including bronze statuettes of praying figures finished with gilded hands.

events.commonsFile: God golden hand-Sb 2823-IMG 0815-gradient.jpg

events.label: Iranian Highland Trade Routes
events.description: Elam straddled the trade routes crossing the Zagros Mountains, the overland link carrying tin, lapis lazuli, and other treasures from Afghanistan and Central Asia down to resource-poor Mesopotamia. Taxing those caravans was a backbone of Elamite wealth.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tin was the prize: you cannot make bronze without it, and the main ancient source was Badakhshan in northern Afghanistan, reached either overland through Elam or by sea via an Indus-Valley outpost called Shortughai. The deep-blue stone lapis lazuli came from the same few Afghan mountains and had to be carried hundreds of miles west. The traffic ran both directions and got specialized fast — by around 2100 BCE the route supported bilingual Sumerian-Elamite glossaries, the earliest surviving evidence of professional translators working between two ancient languages.

events.commonsFile: Indus carnelian beads with white design imported to Susa in 2600-1700 BCE LOUVRE Sb 13099.jpg

events.label: Elamite-Akkadian Treaty
events.description: A clay tablet from Susa, now in the Louvre, records a sworn pact between Akkad and the Elamite king Khita — the oldest surviving full diplomatic treaty in any language anywhere, nearly a thousand years older than the famous Egypt–Hittite peace.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The text is bilingual in spirit: it was composed in the Elamite language but written down in Akkadian cuneiform, the prestige diplomatic script of the day, which is why it doubles as the first written record of Elamite ever found. The Elamite king binds himself with the line "the enemy of Naram-Sin is my enemy, the friend of Naram-Sin is my friend," and the deal reportedly went beyond words — Khita is thought to have sent Elamite troops and married a daughter to the Akkadian king. Crucially, the oath calls Elamite gods as witnesses, which makes this brittle slab our earliest real list of the Elamite pantheon, religion preserved as the small print of a political contract.

events.commonsFile: 2015-12 Traité d'alliance conclu entre Naram-Sin et Khita Sb 8833.jpg

events.label: Naram-Sin Conquers Elam
events.description: Around 2240 BCE the Akkadian king Naram-Sin (Sargon's grandson) campaigned into the Zagros against Elam — and commemorated his mountain victories on the pink sandstone Victory Stele that, ironically, an Elamite king would later steal back to Susa.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The stele was a genuine first in art history: Naram-Sin is shown wearing a horned helmet — the badge of a god — making him the earliest Mesopotamian king to portray himself as divine, towering over his troops as he climbs a mountain across the bodies of fallen Lullubi highlanders. The deeper irony is the object's afterlife: more than a thousand years later Shutruk-Nahhunte hauled this monument to a Zagros conquest back over the Zagros to Susa, then carved his own Elamite boast onto it — the conquered region claiming the conqueror's trophy.

events.commonsFile: Stèle de Naram-Sin - Musée du Louvre Antiquités orientales SB 4 ; AS 6065.jpg

events.label: Linear Elamite Script
events.description: Around the Akkadian period the Elamites built their own writing system from scratch — Linear Elamite, a clean set of roughly 80 signs read left to right, unrelated to Mesopotamian cuneiform. It stumped scholars for over a century until a partial decipherment was proposed in 2022.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Unlike the older, tally-like Proto-Elamite, Linear Elamite looks like it actually spells out the Elamite language, mixing signs for sounds with signs for whole words. The crack came the same way Old Persian was unlocked two centuries earlier: a team led by François Desset spotted repeated sign-clusters at the start of inscriptions, guessed they were royal names like Puzur-Inshushinak, and worked outward from there — leaning on bilingual objects that carry the same dedication in both Akkadian and Linear Elamite. The reading is promising but not yet settled consensus; some specialists are waiting for full text translations before they sign off.

events.commonsFile: Bilingual Linear Elamite Akkadian inscription of king Kutik-Inshushinak Table of the Lion Louvre Museum Sb 17.jpg

events.label: Elamite Cylinder Seals
events.description: Elamite carvers turned the cylinder seal — a small engraved stone rolled across wet clay to leave a signature picture — into something distinctly their own, crowding it with ritual scenes, mythological creatures, and snake imagery that looked nothing like the tidier Mesopotamian style.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: A seal worked like a Bronze Age signature and a lock at once: roll it over a lump of clay sealing a jar or a door, and the unbroken impression proved nobody had tampered with it. The standout Elamite motif is a big bearded serpent and a god enthroned above a snake — a creature that turns up on seals from Susa and other Iranian sites and seems to carry a lost mythology, one scholars have linked to much later Iranian snake-demon legends. The scenes were carved in reverse, intaglio, so that only the rolled-out impression reads correctly — a tiny everyday object doubling as a window into Elamite belief.

events.commonsFile: Susa III or Proto-Elamite cylinder seal 3150-2800 BC Mythological being on a boat Louvre Museum Sb 6379.jpg

events.label: Shimashki Dynasty
events.description: The Shimashki were a highland Elamite royal line, probably named for a region in the southern Zagros mountains, who ruled Elam from roughly 2100 to 1900 BCE. They went from Ur's tribute-paying ally to the dynasty that sacked it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: One historian, Touraj Daryaee, argues the king-list flatters them: Shimashki may have been less a tidy single state than a shifting alliance of Zagros peoples who happened to share a throne-name. They sealed their independence the moment Kindattu burned Ur, after which the temple of Inshushinak at Susa took in votive offerings tagged as 'spoils of Ur.' This is also where the Elamite habit of carrying off conquered cities' god-statues as war trophies begins — a practice that would explode in scale centuries later under Shutruk-Nahhunte.

events.commonsFile: Nude man with weapons Ur III Shimashki dynasty 2000-1940 BC.jpg

events.label: Puzur-Inshushinak
events.description: Puzur-Inshushinak (his name means "Refuge is Inshushinak") was the last great king of the Awan line. As Akkad collapsed around 2100 BCE he seized the moment, pushed into a fractured Mesopotamia, and briefly styled himself a rival emperor — leaving behind the richest stash of Linear Elamite text we have.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He borrowed Naram-Sin's own boast, "king of the four quarters," for himself, a pointed bit of one-upmanship against the dying empire that had twice sacked his capital. His monuments hedge their bets linguistically: many carry the same dedication in both Akkadian (the international language) and the brand-new Linear Elamite (the homegrown one), a deliberate statement that Elam now had a script of its own. One of his most famous dedications survives on a white limestone statue of the goddess Narundi, inscribed on one flank in cuneiform and on the other in Linear Elamite.

events.commonsFile: Puzur-Inshushinak, Governor of Susa, on the statue of the Goddess Narundi.jpg

events.label: Goddess Pinikir
events.description: Pinikir was an old Elamite sky goddess tied to the planet Venus and to love and fertility — the same turf the Mesopotamian Inanna/Ishtar covered. She is one of the oldest named deities we can track in Elam.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: In the Treaty of Naram-Sin around 2250 BCE she is listed first, ahead of some forty other gods — a hint that early Elamite religion gave a goddess the top seat. Over the second millennium her identity got tangled with Ishtar's through the heavy cultural traffic between Susa and Sumer, and she went on to a remarkable second life far from home: she became prominent in Hurrian religion in Anatolia, where bilingual ritual texts from the Hittite capital Hattusa simply equate her name with Ishtar's. Pinikir is probably the deepest, pre-Mesopotamian layer of the Elamite pantheon.

events.commonsFile: Winged deity (Pinikir), ca. 14th–13th century BCE.jpg

events.label: Elamite Cuneiform Adoption
events.description: After the sack of Ur, the Elamite court made a lasting choice: from now on, royal inscriptions and official records would use Mesopotamian cuneiform, awkwardly bent to spell out the Elamite language. The kingdom's older homegrown script was quietly retired.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: That older script was Linear Elamite, a set of geometric signs used since around 2300 BCE; it fell out of use entirely by roughly 1850–1900 BCE and stayed unread until scholars announced a decipherment only in 2022. Cuneiform never fit Elamite comfortably — it was designed for Sumerian and Akkadian, languages with very different sounds — but adopting it plugged Elam into the shared writing world of Near Eastern diplomacy, where Akkadian was about to become the common tongue for the next 1,500 years. The trade-off: Elam became far more culturally porous to Mesopotamian ideas.

events.commonsFile: Tablette elamite lineaire Sb9382.jpg

events.label: Elamite Destruction of Ur
events.description: In about 2004 BCE an Elamite army marched into Ur, the glittering capital of Sumer's last native dynasty, and burned it down. The raid accidentally ended Sumerian political history and put the last Sumerian king in Elamite chains.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Elamite king Kindattu, sixth ruler of the Shimashki line, led the coalition and hauled Ibbi-Sin, the last king of Ur, off to captivity, where he died at an unknown date. The disaster was so searing that Sumerian priests composed the Lament for Ur, a poem voiced by Ningal, the city's grieving goddess, who pleads with the high gods An and Enlil to spare her city and is refused. It is the oldest surviving 'city lament' and a direct literary ancestor of the Book of Lamentations. The Elamites only meant to loot a rival and go home, but the sack let the incoming Amorites flood the plain, and spoken Sumerian never recovered.

events.commonsFile: Lament for ur (cropped).JPG

events.label: Susa Acropolis Temples
events.description: The acropolis at Susa — a raised mound at the heart of the city — held the temple of Inshushinak, the city-god and judge of the dead, alongside other shrines. It was the religious nerve-center of Elam for thousands of years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: French archaeologists dug the acropolis between 1902 and 1908, and the find that anchored the early chronology was almost comically domestic: hidden in the foundations of two sanctuaries were small figurines and tablets, each carrying the same dedication by Shulgi, the Ur III king. Later temple decoration from around 1150 BCE survives too, including glazed-brick reliefs of a bull-man guarding a stylized palm tree. The same mound was reused so continuously that a 13th-century-CE fortress, and the French dig-house built on top of it, still crown the ancient acropolis today.

events.commonsFile: Fragments of decoration from the Temple of Inshushinak, tutelary god of Susa, depicting a bull man and palm tree, from Suse (Iran), around 1150 BC, Louvre Lens, France (26844633192).jpg

events.label: Elamite Royal Succession
events.description: Elamite kingship did not simply pass from father to son. Power rotated through a set of ranked offices — grand regent, viceroy of Elam, viceroy of Susa — so brothers, uncles, and nephews cycled through the top jobs, an arrangement that made the whole royal clan rule as a team.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The system's payoff was that there were almost never weak boy-kings, because an experienced adult relative was always next in line, which cut down on succession crises. The cost was that no single king could build a personal dynasty or chase grand lifelong projects the way an Egyptian pharaoh could. Strikingly, the closest parallel anywhere in the ancient world is Shang dynasty China, whose oracle bones record the same brother-to-brother succession — the two systems almost certainly invented the idea independently, on opposite ends of Asia. The pattern starts loosely here under Shimashki and hardens into Elam's signature institution under the later Sukkalmah kings.

events.commonsFile: Seal of King Ebarat Louvre Museum Sb 6225 (detail of King Ebarat).jpg

events.label: Elamite Copper and Tin Trade
events.description: Bronze is copper plus tin, and Elam sat astride the supply of both — copper from sources around the Gulf and Iranian plateau, tin from Afghanistan. That made Susa's merchants rich and made Elam a chokepoint of the entire Bronze Age economy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The two metals came from completely different directions and had to be brought together, which is exactly why control of the routes was worth so much: whoever moved the tin effectively controlled who could arm an army or cast monumental statues. Elamite workshops turned that incoming metal into real objects — including inscribed copper-alloy foundation pegs that kings buried in temple walls as dedications, often shaped as a figure carrying a builder's basket. These deposits doubled as a permanent record, naming the king and the god the building honored right in the metal.

events.commonsFile: Foundation nail-Sb 2879-P5280608-gradient.jpg

events.label: Sukkalmah Period
events.description: The roughly 400-year stretch (about 1900-1500 BCE) when Elam was run not by a king but by a 'grand regent' (sukkalmah), the standout being a power-sharing setup where three relatives held three ranked offices at once.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Most ancient monarchies broke apart in succession bloodbaths, but the Sukkalmah cleverly dodged that by sharing power across three offices held by brothers and uncles, who rotated upward as each man above them died. The dynasty deliberately skipped the usual Mesopotamian words for 'king' (lugal, sharrum) and styled its ruler as a vizier-servant of the gods instead, a humbler self-image than the god-king next door in Babylon. Scholars still debate the exact shape of the system, with some reading it as one ruler at a time and others as a genuine triumvirate.

events.commonsFile: Men with daggers Sukkalmah dynasty 1940-1600 BCE Susa Louvre Museum Sb 1394.jpg

events.label: Eparti I, Founder of the Sukkalmah
events.description: Eparti I (also spelled Ebarat) was the founder, around 1850 BCE, of the dynasty that ran Elam for the next three-plus centuries through its trademark three-office family government.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Eparti's name survives carved on his own personal cylinder seal, found at Susa and now in the Louvre, which is part of how we can pin a real person to the founding rather than just a king-list entry. There's a wrinkle scholars argue over: an 'Eparti I' and an 'Ebarat II' both appear in the sources, and the credit for actually inventing the sukkalmah three-office structure is often given to the later Ebarat, so the 'founder' label is a bit blurry. Either way, the system he set in motion outlasted him by roughly 300 years, an unusually long run for any Bronze Age dynasty.

events.commonsFile: Seal of King Ebarat Louvre Museum Sb 6225.jpg

events.label: Siwe-palar-hupak and the Mari Letters
events.description: Around 1770 BCE the Elamite ruler Siwe-palar-hupak sat at the top of the Near Eastern pecking order, and the clay letters from the palace at Mari (in modern Syria) caught it in writing: even Hammurabi of Babylon called him 'father.'

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Near Eastern diplomats ranked each other with fake family words, where 'father' meant your superior, 'brother' your equal, and 'son' your inferior, so Hammurabi and Zimri-Lim both calling the Elamite 'father' is a snapshot of Elam outranking Babylon before Hammurabi was famous. Siwe-palar-hupak even led a coalition with both of them that crushed the kingdom of Eshnunna, before he overreached, Hammurabi flipped sides, and Elam was pushed back east. The whole episode is preserved by sheer luck: when Hammurabi sacked Mari in 1759 BCE, the palace fire baked its 25,000 tablets hard enough to survive 3,700 years.

events.commonsFile: P1050763 Louvre code Hammurabi face rwk.JPG

events.label: Kudur-Nahhunte I Invades Babylonia
events.description: Soon after Hammurabi died, the Elamite king Kudur-Nahhunte I (also written Kutir-Nahhunte) poured into a weakened Babylonia, looting cities and hauling sacred temple statues back to Susa.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Carrying off a city's cult statue wasn't just theft; in Mesopotamian belief the god literally lived in the image, so dragging it home meant capturing the enemy's divine protector and humiliating them. The defeat he dealt Hammurabi's son Samsuiluna stung so deeply that the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal was still complaining about a statue of the goddess Nanaya stolen by Elam more than 1,600 years later, when he 'rescued' it in the 600s BCE. This raid set the template for an Elam-versus-Mesopotamia grudge match that flared for the next thousand years, peaking with Shutruk-Nahhunte's sack of Babylon around 1158 BCE.

events.commonsFile: Ishtar Eshnunna Louvre AO12456.jpg

events.label: Humban, King of the Elamite Gods
events.description: Humban was the king of the Elamite gods — the head-of-pantheon figure invoked first in royal inscriptions, addressed as 'the king' and 'the great one.' His name turns up inside dozens of royal names, in the form 'Humban-has-given.'

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Humban's special gift was kitin, an Elamite idea of god-given royal power and divine protection that legitimized whoever sat on the throne — he was the god who made kings. His clout actually grew over time: in the late (Neo-Elamite) period, roughly half of all known kings carried a Humban-name, like Humban-haltash. His main sanctuary stood not at Susa but at Liyan on the Persian Gulf coast, near modern Bushehr, suggesting his cult came from the southern coast and highlands. Humban-names still appear in Persian-era records of the fifth century BCE, long after Elam itself had been absorbed.

events.commonsFile: Kurangun central panel, male and female deities (Inshushinak and Napirisha).jpg

events.label: Kiririsha, the Great Mother
events.description: Kiririsha — her name means 'Great Lady' — was the mother goddess of the Elamite pantheon, called 'mother of the gods' and worshipped alongside the realm's chief gods in the standard divine formulas that opened official texts.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Her cult center, like Humban's, was at the Gulf port of Liyan, where she is documented from the 19th century BCE; near the site, archaeologists found a curious local custom of ritually 'burying' palm trees, tentatively linked to her worship. Her role in royal inscriptions was to protect childbirth and legitimize queens. One nuance the narrative glides past: modern specialists such as Wouter Henkelman and François Vallat actually pair Kiririsha with the god Napirisha, not Humban, and reject the old idea that these god-names were interchangeable — Elamite theology was messier and more regional than a tidy family tree suggests.

events.commonsFile: Statue of Napirasu, SB 2731.jpg

events.label: Nahhunte, the Sun God
events.description: Nahhunte was the Elamite sun god, whose name doubled as the ordinary word for 'sun' and meant something like 'creator of the day.' Like the Mesopotamian Shamash, he was the divine judge who watched over oaths and the law.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He shows up early: in the Treaty of Naram-Sin, the oldest known Elamite text, he is the fifth divine witness called to guarantee the oath. His name became the second great building-block of royal names, behind kings like Shutruk-Nahhunte and Kutir-Nahhunte, casting the ruler as the earthly enforcer of the sun-god's cosmic justice. He was worshipped mainly in the west, around Susa, and curiously appears in writing fairly rarely for so important a god — in legal texts his name often hides behind the shared sun-god symbol that Mesopotamians read as Shamash.

events.commonsFile: Sit-Shamski bronze model from Susa Sb 2743-P5260439-white.jpg

events.label: Tepti-Ahar Tomb Complex
events.description: A royal grave with company. At Haft Tappeh near Susa, the barrel-vaulted baked-brick tomb attached to King Tepti-Ahar's temple held not just royal burials but a hidden adjoining chamber packed with bodies — a window into Middle Elamite death ritual that still unsettles excavators.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tepti-Ahar (late 15th / early 14th century BCE) was likely the last of the transitional Kidinuid kings, and he founded this city, ancient Kabnak, as a new capital. Reached through a low concealed entrance off the king's tomb, the mass grave held around two dozen young people — by some readings a group of young women — laid down together, widely read as retainers or sacrifices accompanying the dead into the afterlife. Other excavated burials at the site run into the hundreds, and scholars still argue over which deaths were ritual and which were the result of an epidemic or massacre.

events.commonsFile: Grabgewölbe Haft Tepe.JPG

events.label: Elamite Astronomical Knowledge
events.description: Elamite priests maintained astronomical observations that contributed to the broader Mesopotamian tradition, with evidence of celestial calculations found in Susa archives.

events.label: Worship of Humban
events.description: Humban, the Elamite sky god and 'king of the gods,' became increasingly prominent in the Middle Elamite period, often paired with Kiririsha, the mother goddess.

events.label: Haft Tappeh Royal City
events.description: The capital before the great ziggurat. Haft Tappeh — ancient Kabnak, near Susa — was a Middle Elamite royal city with monumental brick architecture, craft workshops, and large grain stores, a working seat of power a couple of centuries before Untash-Napirisha built Dur-Untash.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The mounds (Haft Tappeh means "seven hills" in Persian) have given up an unusually intimate slice of Elamite life: clay-tablet archives, an artisans' quarter with kilns and metal- and bone-working debris, and even practice tablets where trainee scribes drilled their cuneiform signs. Among the finds are vivid painted terracotta funerary heads, their eyes and headdresses still picked out in color. The site only came to light in the 1960s when a modern sugarcane road cut straight through the ancient city, exposing its buried walls.

events.commonsFile: Keramik aus Iran, Elamisches Totenportrait, Haft Tappe, um 1250 v.C. (3).jpg

events.label: Igihalkid Dynasty
events.description: The royal line that hauled Elam back to the top table. Named for its founder Ige-halki, the Igihalkid kings (roughly 1400–1210 BCE) rebuilt the army, refortified Susa, and turned a quiet provincial kingdom into one of the Late Bronze Age's great powers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Igihalkids practiced something close to dynastic insurance: kings repeatedly married into the Kassite royal house ruling Babylon, so an Elamite prince could one day claim a Babylonian throne by blood. That gamble paid off spectacularly in the next generation, when Elam used exactly such a claim as the pretext to sack Babylon and carry off its treasures. The family kept the throne for nearly two centuries by passing it brother-to-brother as often as father-to-son, which helped them avoid the child-king succession crises that wrecked other Bronze Age dynasties.

events.commonsFile: Untash king Axe.jpg

events.label: Humban-Numena I
events.description: Humban-Numena was a Middle Elamite king of the Igihalkid line in the mid-1300s BCE who launched the great temple-building program that his successor carried to its peak. His inscriptions, in cuneiform Elamite, helped fix that script as the standard royal hand.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He left dedications at both Susa and the Gulf temple of Liyan, and he married a daughter of the Kassite king of Babylon, knitting Elam into the great-power diplomacy of the age (most sources make him the father, not the grandfather, of Untash-Napirisha). It was that son, Untash-Napirisha, who built Chogha Zanbil — a vast walled ziggurat complex meant as a new religious capital for all Elam — the monumental culmination of the program Humban-Numena's generation set in motion. Chogha Zanbil still stands today as one of the best-preserved ziggurats anywhere and Iran's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.commonsFile: The east side of the ziggurat, Chogha Zanbil, Iran (47780495562).jpg

events.label: Elamite Bronze Statue of Napir-Asu
events.description: Two tons of metal cast to last forever. The headless bronze statue of Queen Napir-Asu — wife of Untash-Napirisha — stands about four and a half feet tall in court dress, hands folded, skirt rendered as woven fabric, and it weighs an astonishing 3,760 pounds (1,750 kg). Found at Susa in 1903, it is the masterwork of Elamite metalcasting.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It is heavy on purpose. Most ancient bronze figures are hollow shells over a clay core, which saves metal and money; Napir-Asu's makers instead cast a copper-and-bronze outer shell, scooped out the core, and then filled the entire hollow with molten bronze — turning a statue into a near-solid metal ingot in human form. The reason is spelled out in the cuneiform curse running around her skirt: anyone who smashes the figure or erases her name is to be struck down by the gods Napirisha, Kiririsha, and Inshushinak. Making it un-melt-able was the queen's insurance against a future king recycling her bronze, and it worked — she survived every sacking of Susa for three millennia, losing only her head.

events.commonsFile: Napir Asu 1.jpg

events.label: Untash-Napirisha
events.description: The king who out-built everyone. Untash-Napirisha (ruled roughly 1275–1240 BCE) was the greatest of the Igihalkid rulers, and he poured Elam's wealth into the largest monument-building program in its history — a whole new sacred city crowned by the ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His name means roughly "Untash is (the god) Napirisha" — and he made that personal god the co-owner of his great ziggurat, deliberately pairing the highland deity Napirisha with Inshushinak, the lowland lord of Susa. That was political theology: Elam was always an uneasy marriage of mountain and plain, and Untash-Napirisha tried to fuse the two halves' gods into a single state cult at one site. He stamped his name into the bricks by the thousand, so that three thousand years later archaeologists could still read the builder's signature straight off the surviving wall faces.

events.commonsFile: Glazed (originally blue) door plaque with boss. The Elamite cuneiform inscription reads "Palace of Untash-Napirisha, King of Elam". 13th centiury BCE. From Choga Zanbil, Iran. British Museum.jpg

events.label: Ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil
events.description: The biggest ziggurat left standing on Earth. Built around 1250 BCE as the centerpiece of Untash-Napirisha's new city of Dur-Untash, this five-stepped mud-brick tower — a Mesopotamian temple-mountain form done bigger than any Mesopotamian original — is the best-preserved ziggurat anywhere and Iran's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: What saved it was the skin. Where Mesopotamian ziggurats wore mostly sun-dried mud brick and slumped into shapeless mounds, Chogha Zanbil's builders cased the whole exterior in fuel-hungry kiln-fired brick — far costlier, far tougher — so the outer face survived 3,000 years of weather. It once rose about 174 feet (53 meters); erosion has worn it down to roughly 80 feet (25 meters) today. The site was lost until 1935, when an oil surveyor flying over Khuzestan spotted a suspiciously square mound; full excavation under Roman Ghirshman from the 1950s turned up thousands of bricks that had never been laid, hinting the great complex was abandoned before it was ever finished.

events.commonsFile: Choqa Zanbil 2.jpg

events.label: Elamite Warrior Traditions
events.description: Elam's soldiers had a fearsome reputation across the ancient Near East — celebrated archers and charioteers whose mountain-bred tactics repeatedly gave lowland Mesopotamian armies fits.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: We mostly see them through enemy eyes: the most vivid surviving images of Elamite troops are Assyrian palace reliefs, carved centuries later, that show them being slaughtered at the Battle of Til-Tuba — bodies, broken chariots, and fleeing bowmen choking a river. Even in defeat the bow dominates the scene, a backhanded tribute to what the Elamites were known for. Their edge came from terrain as much as weapons: the Zagros passes that funneled their raids into Babylonia also gave them a highland refuge no flatland army could easily follow them into.

events.commonsFile: Relief Humiliation of Elamite Kings Nineveh Gypsum N Palace Ashurbanipal British Museum MH.jpg

events.label: Shutruk-Nahhunte
events.description: The Elamite king (reigned roughly 1184–1155 BCE) who founded the Shutrukid dynasty and pulled off the greatest art heist of the ancient world — looting Babylon and dragging its treasures, the Code of Hammurabi included, home over the mountains to Susa.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He didn't just steal the monuments — he defaced them. On the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin he had his scribes carve a fresh Elamite inscription right onto the thousand-year-old Akkadian masterpiece, bragging that he had taken it. He justified the whole invasion with a legal fiction: the Shutrukids claimed descent from a Kassite princess who had married into the Elamite line, so Shutruk-Nahhunte framed the attack not as conquest but as a rightful heir collecting a throne he was owed.

events.commonsFile: Shutruk-Nakhunte, Musée du Louvre.jpg

events.label: Elamite Sack of Babylon
events.description: Elam's 1158 BCE smash-and-grab on Babylon — the army breached the walls in weeks, then methodically stripped the temples and palaces and hauled the loot back east on carts. Among the trophies: the Code of Hammurabi and the Stele of Naram-Sin.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Elamites didn't torch Babylon (it was rebuilt within a generation) — they wanted the prestige objects intact. The single most aggressive act wasn't burning anything; it was seizing the cult statue of Marduk, Babylon's chief god, which signaled that the god had abandoned the city. There's a strange upside to the theft: the Code of Hammurabi survives today only because it was carried to Susa. Left in its temple at Sippar, the tall block of black stone would almost certainly have been smashed in a later war or recycled for its valuable stone.

events.commonsFile: P1050763 Louvre code Hammurabi face rwk.JPG

events.label: Kutir-Nahhunte III
events.description: Shutruk-Nahhunte's son, who pushed the family's Babylonian wars to their peak — installing Elamite governors over Mesopotamian cities and, for about a decade, ruling a genuine two-region empire straddling both sides of the Zagros mountains.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The "III" is a modern bookkeeping trick — scholars number him to tell him apart from earlier kings of the same name; the Elamites never numbered their own rulers. This decade (roughly 1155–1145 BCE) is the closest Elam ever came to actually governing Mesopotamia rather than just raiding it, but the empire was thinner than it looked. Elamite administration never sank the deep roots that the Akkadian or Assyrian systems did, which is exactly why it unraveled so fast once Babylon found a leader to fight back.

events.commonsFile: Statue de Manishtusu - Sb 47 - Antiquités orientales du Louvre.jpg

events.label: Sit Shamshi Bronze Tableau
events.description: A cast-bronze tabletop model about 23 inches long (60 cm) showing a dawn ritual frozen in metal: two nude priests at a miniature temple, one crouching to pour water, surrounded by tiny altars, basins, a ziggurat, and bronze tree-trunks.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Its name means "sunrise," and the inscription on the base has Shilhak-Inshushinak calling it "my bronze sunrise" — a personal offering to the god Inshushinak. What makes it priceless is that it freezes a ceremony in mid-action: most ancient art shows kings and gods posing, but this captures the plumbing of actual worship, down to the water being poured. It's the clearest surviving snapshot of what an ordinary morning inside an Elamite temple genuinely looked like.

events.commonsFile: Sit-Shamski bronze model from Susa 8873.jpg

events.label: Shilhak-Inshushinak
events.description: The last great Elamite power-king (reigned roughly 1150–1120 BCE) — Shutruk-Nahhunte's other son, a relentless builder and warrior who kept the Babylonian wars going and left Elam's most famous bronze, the Sit Shamshi.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His name translates roughly as "he who multiplies," with the city-god Inshushinak tacked on — and he lived up to it, blanketing Susa in temple construction. His most useful legacy to historians isn't a battle but his restoration inscriptions: when he repaired old shrines, his scribes carefully listed the long-dead kings who had built them first. Those name-lists are some of our best evidence for reconstructing the otherwise murky sequence of earlier Elamite dynasties — an ancient king accidentally writing the family tree for us.

events.commonsFile: P1050576 Louvre Oblélisque de Manishtusu rwk.JPG

events.label: Hutelutush-Inshushinak
events.description: The king who inherited the collapse (reigned around 1120–1110 BCE) — Shilhak-Inshushinak's son, who took over a kingdom stretched too thin and promptly lost it to a resurgent Babylon, then fled into the highlands as the lowlands fell away.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He inherited the bill, not the glory: an overextended army, a treasury drained by his father's building sprees, and a Babylon now organized for revenge. When Nebuchadnezzar I sacked Susa and reclaimed the Marduk statue, Hutelutush-Inshushinak escaped to Anshan in the mountains and ruled a shrunken rump kingdom. After him Elam goes almost completely dark in the records for nearly three centuries — a "dark age" so quiet that even Mesopotamian chronicles barely mention it.

events.commonsFile: Statue de Napir-Asu - Musée du Louvre - Antiquités orientales SB 2731.jpg

events.label: Nebuchadnezzar I Defeats Elam
events.description: The Babylonian comeback. Around 1110 BCE Nebuchadnezzar I (the first of the name, six centuries before the famous one) marched on Elam, sacked Susa, and dragged the stolen Marduk statue home — ending Elam's golden age.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His whole reign turned on recovering one object: the cult statue of Marduk, whose absence had left Babylon religiously humiliated. He got it back — and the victory was celebrated so loudly that it likely helped cement Marduk's rise to the top of the Babylonian pantheon. But he either couldn't find or didn't bother with the older trophies: the Code of Hammurabi and the Naram-Sin stele stayed buried at Susa, which is the only reason archaeologists were there to dig them up three thousand years later.

events.commonsFile: Detail, Kudurru of Ritti-Marduk, from Sippar, Iraq, 1125-1104 BCE. British Museum.jpg

events.label: Neo-Elamite Revival
events.description: Elam's long second act (roughly 1100–539 BCE) — no longer one centralized empire but a loose patchwork of highland and lowland city-kingdoms, each with its own royal line, all still calling themselves Elamite and all stuck living next door to a rising Assyria.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: These kings survived by playing the great-power game: in the late 8th century BCE the Elamite king Huban-nikash I threw his army behind the Babylonian rebel Merodach-baladan against the Assyrian king Sargon II — the opening move in a tug-of-war over Babylon that ran for generations. It was a fragmented age that left almost no grand royal monuments, yet it could still produce dazzling wealth: a Neo-Elamite tomb at Jubaji yielded gold bracelets and discs of breathtaking craftsmanship, proof the old culture was far from dead. Much of what we know about these centuries comes not from royal boasts but from clay administrative archives dug up on the acropolis at Susa — thousands of ordinary names recording a kingdom still quietly running its books.

events.commonsFile: Golden-Bracelet,Jubaji,Rahm-Hormoz,Khuzestan,Iran-Neo-Elamite-Period-CA-585-539-BC.jpg

events.label: King of Anshan
events.description: "King of Anshan" was the old Elamite royal title for the highland capital up on the Iranian plateau — and after Elam fell, an incoming line of Persian rulers grabbed it as their own. By the time of Cyrus the Great, the founder of the Persian Empire was officially calling himself heir to an Elamite throne.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: We can put a physical object behind this. The seal of Cyrus I (Cyrus the Great's grandfather) carries an Elamite inscription naming him "Cyrus the Anshanite, son of Teispes," and it survives because scribes were still pressing it into clay during the reign of Darius I — roughly 150 years after Cyrus I lived. In other words the Persian court kept the dead king's signet as a working heirloom for a century and a half, stamping it onto everyday administrative tablets. The picture cut into it is a Persian horseman spearing fallen enemies, the standard royal-warrior image of the highland nobility.

events.commonsFile: Cyrus I seal.png

events.label: Te-Umman and the Battle of Til-Tuba
events.description: The 653 BCE bloodbath where Ashurbanipal's Assyrians shattered the army of the Elamite king Te-Umman — then carved the whole battle, blow by gory blow, across a palace wall like an ancient comic strip. The reliefs survive in the British Museum, and they are some of the most violent images to come out of the ancient world.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ashurbanipal's annals claim Te-Umman was doomed before a sword was drawn: the gods supposedly struck him with a seizure and sent a lunar eclipse as a warning, omens the king ignored. The relief is read panel to panel like a film reel — the Elamites are driven down a hill and into the River Ulai until the water is clogged with corpses, and Te-Umman's severed head reappears in scene after scene as it is carried home, including the famous garden banquet where it hangs in a tree above the feasting king. The Assyrian soldier who actually did the beheading isn't anonymous, either: the texts record that the man who delivered the head to Nineveh was singled out and rewarded for it.

events.commonsFile: Battle of Ulai (composite).jpg

events.label: Elamite Alliance with Shamash-shum-ukin
events.description: Ashurbanipal's older brother and the king of Babylon — and the man whose 652 BCE revolt the Elamites bet on, and lost. Backing the wrong brother is the decision that finished off Elam.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Their father Esarhaddon had split the empire to keep the peace: Ashurbanipal got Assyria and the senior role, Shamash-shum-ukin got Babylon as a junior, closely watched king. The arrangement held for about seventeen years before the elder brother, tired of playing second, raised a coalition — Elamites, Chaldeans, Arameans, and others — and declared Babylon free. It failed spectacularly: Ashurbanipal besieged Babylon for years, starved it, and took it in 648 BCE, and Shamash-shum-ukin died in his burning palace — though ancient sources are vague enough that scholars still debate whether it was suicide, execution, or accident.

events.commonsFile: Detail of a stone monument of Shamash-shum-ukin as a basket-bearer. 668-655 BCE. From the temple of Nabu at Borsippa, Iraq and is currently housed in the British Museum.jpg

events.label: Sack of Susa
events.description: In 646 BCE the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal smashed Susa, leveled its temples, and scattered salt over the ruins — the ancient way of cursing a place so nothing would grow back. He bragged in his inscriptions of total annihilation, and with it the independent Elamite kingdom was finished.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ashurbanipal went a chilling step further: he had the bones of long-dead Elamite kings dug out of their tombs and carted off to Assyria, a deliberate attack on their afterlife meant to deny their ghosts any rest. He also looted the great temple of the chief Elamite god Inshushinak and dragged its statue back to Nineveh, and his reliefs gloat over the wreckage. Yet the irony runs underneath the whole chapter — within a generation Susa was being rebuilt as a Persian capital, and the language Ashurbanipal thought he had buried would go on running the largest empire the world had yet seen.

events.commonsFile: Destruction of the Elamite city of Hamanu 645-635 BCE.jpg

events.label: Elamite Legacy in Persia
events.description: When the Persians built their empire they didn't bulldoze the Elamite past — they moved into it. They made the old Elamite city of Susa one of their royal capitals, kept Elamite as an official language, and ran their paperwork on Elamite scribal methods. The conquerors quietly became the heirs.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The most dazzling thing the Persians left at Susa is the Frieze of Archers, a wall of life-size guardsmen built up from molded, brightly glazed bricks (sometimes identified with the royal bodyguard the Greeks called the Immortals). It's a telling mash-up: the figures are Persian, the glazed-brick technique is borrowed straight from Babylonian Mesopotamia, and the whole thing decorated a palace in an ancient Elamite city. Darius's own foundation charter at Susa actually brags about the gold from Lydia, the cedar from Lebanon, and the craftsmen from across the empire he pulled in to build it — an empire assembling itself out of everyone it had absorbed.

events.commonsFile: Archers frieze Darius 1st Palace Suse Louvre AOD 488 a.jpg

events.label: Behistun Inscription in Elamite
events.description: High on a cliff in western Iran, Darius I carved a giant billboard of his own greatness — the Behistun Inscription, around 520 BCE, telling how he crushed his rivals and seized the throne. He had it written three times in three languages, and the Elamite version was carved first, a quiet sign of how much the language still mattered.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The inscription sits about 330 feet (100 meters) up a sheer limestone face, deliberately too high to vandalize — which is exactly why copying it became an act of mountaineering. In the late 1830s and 1840s the British officer Henry Rawlinson dangled on ropes off the cliff to take paper squeezes of the text, and decoding its simpler Old Persian column became the key that unlocked all cuneiform, making Behistun the Rosetta Stone of the ancient Near East. Reading the Elamite column stayed harder, because Elamite is a language isolate with no living relatives to cross-check against.

events.commonsFile: Behistun Darius the Great.jpg

events.label: Persepolis Fortification Archive
events.description: Buried in the fortification walls at Persepolis was a filing cabinet of the ancient world: about 30,000 clay tablets logging the Persian court's day-to-day spending — barley rations, workers' wages, travel expenses — from 509 to 494 BCE. The jaw-dropper is that they're written in Elamite, the language of the kingdom Persia had supposedly swallowed whole.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The reason is almost mundane: the Persians inherited Susa and Anshan's scribal schools, which never stopped turning out new Elamite-cuneiform clerks, so the empire just kept hiring the staff it already had. The tablets survived because the fortification wall they sat in collapsed and sealed them under rubble (Alexander the Great's burning of Persepolis in 330 BCE seems to have triggered that collapse rather than directly baking them). Most of the hoard was shipped to the University of Chicago in the 1930s for study and is still being read and gradually returned to Iran — and the tablets carry one of the great bodies of Achaemenid-era seal impressions, making them a goldmine for art historians as well as accountants.

events.commonsFile: Persepolis tablet.jpg
